steps.prompt: Someone walks up to you and says, “Because the bus broke down.” Then they walk away. What’s missing? How do you feel?

cards.title: Linking words that lean
cards.body: A subordinating conjunction starts a part of a sentence that can’t stand alone: because, although, though, since, when, while, if, unless, until, before, after, as, once, even though, so that. That part (a dependent clause) leans on a main idea.

cards.title: What they show
cards.text:
Reason: because, since → We stayed in because it rained.
Contrast: although, even though → Although it rained, we played.
Condition: if, unless → Unless you hurry, you’ll miss it.
Time: when, while, after, before, until → We waited until the bell rang.
cards.note: In essays, these words show how your ideas connect. That makes your reasoning easy to follow.

cards.title: The comma rule
cards.body: If the sentence starts with the linking part, put a comma where it ends: “When the bell rang, we ran outside.” If the main idea comes first, you usually don’t need a comma: “We ran outside when the bell rang.”

cards.title: Don’t leave it hanging
cards.telling: I missed the bus. Because I woke up late.
cards.showing: I missed the bus because I woke up late.
cards.note: A “because” part on its own is a fragment. Join it to its main idea.

prompts: Which linking word made your argument strongest? Why?
How can you tell when a sentence starting with “Because” is only half a sentence?
